hook_text: Hydrogen sulfide is nearly double water's weight — and boils at minus 60. Water holds out to plus 100. The secret is a handshake.
clip_script: Chemistry has a scandal, and it lives in your kettle. Hydrogen sulfide: the same bent shape as water, the same chemical family, nearly TWICE the mass. It boils at minus sixty. Water — smaller, lighter — holds on to plus one hundred. Why does the lightweight refuse to let go? Because boiling never breaks molecules; it breaks the GRIP between them. Think bricks and mortar: the bonds inside a molecule are bricks, the forces between molecules are mortar, and heat only ever attacks the mortar. Mortar comes in three grades. Grade one, the flicker: electron clouds sloshing, giving every molecule a split-second charged tip — weak alone, but it stacks up, which is why bulky wax molecules stand solid while small ones drift as gas. Grade two, the permanent lean: polar molecules lining up plus against minus. Grade three, the handshake: hydrogen bonded to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine locks onto the next molecule's lone pair. That's the hydrogen bond — and water is laced with them. Hydrogen sulfide can't shake hands; sulfur isn't fierce enough. So water grips on to a hundred degrees while its heavier cousin boils away in a freezer. No handshake, no oceans, no rivers, no tea. The entire wet world hangs off grade three grip.
visual_style: A boxing-poster face-off between a small glowing water molecule and a bulky hydrogen sulfide molecule; a brick wall whose mortar glows and crumbles under heat while the bricks stay whole; three escalating grip animations — flicker, lean, handshake — closing on an ocean stitched together by tiny glowing handshakes.
mood: Underdog sports story — the lightweight that wins on grip.
pacing: Punchy face-off open, three-beat climb through the grip grades, sweeping wide-shot finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain any boiling point on sight.
